transcript: A director resigns in controversy as a theater company spirals in a crisis of identity All over some lights and microphones? Welcome to another episode of overthinking theater throwback, where I do retrospectives on recent theater history. In 2016, Shakespeare’s Globe theater in London hired Emma Rice as their new artistic director. Important context: this is a non-profit theater company that operates out of a historically accurate replica of the Globe theater where the majority of Shakespeare’s plays were originally performed. The replica was built in 1997 with the intention of representing for audiences what it was like to attend one of these Elizabethan stage productions as accurately as possible - within reason. Remind me to make another video about why they had to make the floor out of concrete, because it's a hilarious fun fact. But anyway, part of the ethos behind this was the use of unamplified sound as well as what they called “shared light.” As in: the lights could be artificial for evening performances, but the audience would not be in darkness. Emma Rice, however, has much more modern sensibilities, known at the time for spearheading the popular company Kneehigh, which tended to have flashier spectacle and tech. So when she had them install modern theatrical lighting and sound amplification for her early productions at the Globe, it caused quite the uproar, to the point where only 6 months into her tenure, it was announced that she would be stepping down. Rice later told the Guardian, “I don't think they imagined i'd leave.” “They thought i'd accept the new guidelines,” “that i'd want the job more than my practice.” And now, ten years after the incident, the debate remains: who was right? I was studying abroad in London at the time, and I got to see several Globe productions under Rice’s watch, including her Midsummer Night’s Dream, and a Kneehigh co-production called 946: the amazing story of Adolphus Tips, both of which, a fun fact, starred and Ncuti Gatwa before he was famous. My classmates and I were pretty exhilarated by these productions. They were highly entertaining and fostered a fun, communal viewing experience. At one point in Midsummer, they all sang Space Oddity by David Bowie, and while it might have been a far cry from a historical replica of Elizabethan of theatre there was a different kind of kinship on a more fundamental level. Shakespeare's plays, after all, were considered populist entertainment at the time, using modern stagecraft, song and dance and design, even when the play might have taken place centuries earlier. And by that metric, what Emma Rice was doing was a closer spiritual equivalent to what Shakespeare’s original audiences might have experienced. And if this theater company wanted to remain relevant, they needed to embrace that fact. At the time, I was willing to die on that hill, that the Globe was fully in the wrong and Emma Rice had been artistically stifled at best, and unfairly ousted at worst. In retrospect, I can admit that it might be a bit more complicated. In the US at least (and I imagine it's similar in the UK) Non-profits risk losing their benefits if they stray too far from their mission statement, so there was potentially more at stake here than just keeping a bunch of fuddy duddies un-scandalized. Especially for an organization that does, in fairness, place a lot of emphasis on historical education. Still, it's just a shame that Rice seemed to have been set up to fail. But in the end, I guess it worked out for everyone. Emma Rice started a new theater company called Wise Children, where she has all the artistic freedom she wants. And for what it's worth, the Globe’s mission statement remains uncompromised. But even still, the question remains if that's really for the best in the long run. Is the Globe dooming itself to become a dusty relic on the shelf of an otherwise vibrant theater ecosystem? And if so, will it become harder to inspire new generations to take an interest in Shakespeare the way they want to?
